title: ADHD Can Remain Hidden for Decades: New Study Reveals Scale of Underdiagnosis in England
excerpt: Researchers from UCL, Liverpool, and King's College London found that just 1.19% of English patients had a recorded ADHD diagnosis — against an estimated true prevalence of 3 to 5 percent.
body:
A major new study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Europe has laid bare the extent of ADHD underdiagnosis in England, finding that the condition may be going unrecognised in the majority of people who have it — particularly older adults and women.

The research, led by academics at University College London, the University of Liverpool, and King's College London, analysed primary care records covering millions of patients across England. It found that just 1.19% of the population had a recorded ADHD diagnosis, far below the 3 to 5 percent prevalence rate that international epidemiological studies have consistently estimated.

Older Adults: A Lost Generation of Diagnoses

The gap was starkest among older adults. Only 0.05% of patients aged over 65 had a recorded ADHD diagnosis — implying that roughly 93.5% of over-65s with the condition have never been formally identified. For a neurodevelopmental condition that affects executive function, emotional regulation, and daily task management, this represents decades of people navigating work, relationships, and daily life without understanding why certain things felt harder than they should.

"ADHD doesn't develop in adulthood — these are people who have had it their entire lives," said Dr. Amber John, the study's lead author, who moved from UCL to the University of Liverpool during the research. "The diagnostic infrastructure simply didn't exist for most of their lifetimes, and even now, recognition in older populations is extremely limited."

The Gender Gap

The study also highlighted a persistent gender disparity. Boys under 18 are diagnosed at significantly higher rates than girls, a pattern consistent with decades of clinical bias toward the hyperactive-impulsive presentation of ADHD — which is more common in males — over the inattentive subtype, which predominates in females.

However, the data revealed an encouraging shift: diagnosis rates among adult women have increased markedly since 2020, suggesting growing clinical awareness that ADHD in women often manifests differently. Women with ADHD are more likely to present with inattention, disorganisation, and emotional dysregulation rather than the stereotypical hyperactivity that has historically defined the condition in clinical training.

Scale of the Waiting Crisis

The findings arrive amid a referral crisis that is overwhelming NHS services. Recent data shows more than 683,000 outstanding ADHD referrals in England as of March 2026, with waiting times for assessment routinely exceeding two to three years in many regions. An estimated 2.5 million people in the UK are believed to have ADHD, meaning the healthcare system is contending with both a diagnostic backlog and a fundamental capacity shortfall.

"We're seeing a positive trend in that more people are seeking assessment, but the services haven't scaled to meet the demand," said Professor Joshua Stott of UCL, the study's senior author. "There's a real risk that people who finally recognise their symptoms are then left waiting years for confirmation and support."

Why It Matters Beyond the Clinic

Undiagnosed ADHD carries measurable consequences. Research has consistently linked untreated ADHD to higher rates of anxiety, depression, substance misuse, relationship breakdown, workplace underperformance, and accidental injury. For older adults in particular, ADHD symptoms can be misattributed to cognitive decline or dismissed as personality traits, compounding the impact.

The Lancet study's authors recommend expanding diagnostic capacity, improving clinician training — particularly in recognising ADHD in women and older adults — and developing screening tools that can be deployed in primary care settings rather than requiring specialist referral.

For the millions of people who may be living with undiagnosed ADHD, the study's core message is both validating and urgent: the condition doesn't disappear with age, and neither should the effort to identify and support those who have it.
